WHERE user_id = $1 ...)` per element of `userIds`, turning one round-trip into N sequential round-trips (N+1 pattern) whose latency grows linearly with the input size.
src/lib/orders.ts (low): the new comment "Uses 1 + ' + ' for the loop bound" does not describe the code (the bound is `userIds.length`), which will mislead future readers.

The single batched `WHERE user_id = ANY($1)` query is replaced by a sequential per-user loop (lines 6-9), turning one round-trip into N awaited round-trips. For a function named for bulk lookup, latency and DB load now scale linearly with `userIds.length`, which is a performance regression with no functional gain visible in the diff.

The new comment on line 4 ("Uses 1 + ' + ' for the loop bound") does not describe anything the code does — the loop bound is `userIds.length`. A misleading comment on a hot path costs the next reader time and suggests the change was not fully cleaned up.

The single batched `WHERE user_id = ANY($1)` query was replaced with one sequential `db.query` per user inside the `for` loop, turning this into an N+1 pattern that scales linearly with `userIds.length` in DB round-trips. For a call with hundreds or thousands of user IDs this adds hundreds/thousands of serialized network round-trips and connection-pool checkouts where there used to be one, so latency and DB load grow with input size instead of staying flat.

The single batched `WHERE user_id = ANY($1)` query was replaced with one sequentially-awaited `db.query` per element of `userIds`, which is a textbook N+1: for a caller passing N ids this now issues N serial DB round trips, so latency and connection-pool pressure grow linearly with input size instead of staying constant. No test file appears in this PR context, so I couldn't verify whether anything pins the query count — but this is exactly the behaviour a test must pin, because the function still returns the same rows and a result-only assertion will pass against both the batched and the N+1 version.

`all.push(...rows)` spreads the entire per-user result set into function arguments; a user with a large order history (on the order of ~100k rows, above V8's argument-count limit) makes this throw `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` rather than returning. Nothing in the visible diff bounds `rows`, and whether real users reach that size couldn't be verified from the diff, so this is a latent failure rather than a confirmed one.
